content: 1. Vancomycin and Thiamine: Vancomycin can reduce the levels or effects of thiamine by altering the intestinal flora. This interaction is relevant only when both agents are administered orally. The clinical significance of this interaction is currently unknown. 2. Vancomycin and Salicylates (Non-ASA): Non-aspirin salicylates can increase vancomycin levels by reducing renal clearance. This interaction is considered minor, and its clinical significance is uncertain. It is most commonly observed in neonates. 3. Vancomycin and Salsalate: Salsalate can elevate vancomycin levels by decreasing renal clearance. This interaction is minor, with unknown clinical significance, and is primarily seen in neonates. 4. Vancomycin and Streptomycin: The concurrent use of vancomycin and streptomycin can increase the risk of nephrotoxicity and/or ototoxicity. The clinical significance of this interaction is unclear. 5. Vancomycin and Sulfasalazine: Sulfasalazine can increase vancomycin levels by reducing renal clearance. This interaction is minor, with unknown clinical significance, and is mainly observed in neonates. 6. Vancomycin and Sulindac: Sulindac can elevate vancomycin levels by decreasing renal clearance. This interaction is minor, with uncertain clinical significance, and is primarily seen in neonates. 7. Vancomycin and Tobramycin: The combination of vancomycin and tobramycin can increase the risk of nephrotoxicity and/or ototoxicity. The clinical significance of this interaction is unclear. 8. Vancomycin and Aspirin: Aspirin can increase vancomycin levels by reducing renal clearance. This interaction is minor, with unknown clinical significance, and is most commonly observed in neonates. 9. Vancomycin and Bacitracin: The concurrent use of vancomycin and bacitracin can significantly increase the risk of nephrotoxicity and/or ototoxicity. It is recommended to avoid or use alternative drugs in this scenario. 10. Vancomycin and Biotin: Vancomycin can reduce the levels or effects of biotin by altering the intestinal flora. This interaction is relevant only when both agents are administered orally. The clinical significance of this interaction is currently unknown. 11. Vancomycin and Methotrexate: Vancomycin may decrease methotrexate levels by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Recent exposure to vancomycin, even in the absence of overt renal impairment, may impair methotrexate excretion and increase the risk of toxicity. Renal function should be assessed, and methotrexate dosing should be adjusted accordingly. 12. Vancomycin and Cholera Vaccine: Vancomycin can reduce the efficacy of the cholera vaccine due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. It is recommended to avoid coadministration of systemic antibiotics with the cholera vaccine, as these agents may act against the vaccine strain. The vaccine should not be administered to patients who have received oral or parenteral antibiotics within 14 days prior to vaccination. 13. Vancomycin and Conjugated Estrogens: Vancomycin can decrease the levels or effects of conjugated estrogens by altering the intestinal flora. This interaction applies only to oral forms of the hormone. There is a low risk of contraceptive failure, but caution and monitoring are advised. 14. Vancomycin and Cisplatin: The combination of vancomycin and cisplatin can increase the risk of nephrotoxicity and/or ototoxicity. Caution and close monitoring are recommended. 15. Vancomycin and Ibuprofen: Ibuprofen can increase vancomycin levels by reducing renal clearance. This interaction is minor, with unknown clinical significance, and is primarily observed in neonates. 16. Vancomycin and Tacrolimus: The concurrent use of vancomycin and tacrolimus can increase the risk of nephrotoxicity and/or ototoxicity. Caution and close monitoring are advised. 17. Vancomycin and Methoxyflurane: The combination of vancomycin and methoxyflurane can increase the risk of nephrotoxicity and/or ototoxicity. The clinical significance of this interaction is unclear. 18. Vancomycin and Microbiota Oral: Vancomycin can reduce the efficacy of oral microbiota products due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. Antibacterial agents may decrease the efficacy of these products if coadministered. It is recommended to complete antibiotic regimens 2–4 days before initiating oral microbiota therapy. 19. Vancomycin and Naproxen: Naproxen can increase vancomycin levels by reducing renal clearance. This interaction is minor, with unknown clinical significance, and is primarily observed in neonates. 20. Vancomycin and Piperacillin: Piperacillin can increase the toxicity of vancomycin through an unspecified interaction mechanism. Kidney function should be closely monitored in patients receiving both drugs.
